articles.title: The Legal Battle Over Who Gets To Show Their Genitals at a Nude Spa Takes an Unexpected Turn
articles.content:
The Washington State Human Rights Commission (WSHRC) voted last month to permit businesses to set entry requirements based on genitalia when nudity is a core part of the operation—thus allowing, say, an all-female nude establishment to reject customers with male genitals without having to fear anti-discrimination enforcement from the state.
This is not a sentence you necessarily see every day. But it is the latest plot twist related to the legal odyssey that is Olympus Spa v. Armstrong, a case concerning a nude spa that has been embroiled in a yearslong, ever-crescendoing fight with the state after it declined to admit a preoperative transgender woman to its location in Lynnwood, Washington.
The legal question at issue: Did it have the right to do that? It's one that Olympus Spa has asked the Supreme Court to answer.
Haven Wilvich, who has identified as a "nonbinary trans woman," filed a complaint with the WSHRC in 2020, alleging Olympus Spa—a traditional Korean establishment that requires nudity in its pool area and thus caters to a single-sex clientele—had violated the Washington State Law Against Discrimination (WLAD). That statute bars discrimination on the basis of several characteristics, including sexual orientation, which is defined under the law to encompass "heterosexuality, homosexuality, bisexuality, and gender expression or identity."
That last part has proven thorny for the spa. When the business sued on First Amendment grounds, it fared poorly. "We are not unmindful of the concerns and beliefs raised by the Spa," wrote Judge M. Margaret McKeown for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit last year. But the First Amendment, the court said, did not provide an avenue to address those concerns. The government's "objection to the entrance policy was not based on 'disagreement with the message it conveys' but rather with the practice it described—a practice that was unlawful under WLAD," said McKeown. The WSHRC, in other words, did not compel the business to change its beliefs; it was instead enforcing a law as written. Olympus Spa "simply did not challenge the statute itself," McKeown noted, "and it is not our role to rewrite the statute."
As unsatisfying as this was to many onlookers, it was also likely correct under current law. "Generally speaking, the [Supreme] Court has been reluctant to allow businesses to say, 'We get to associate with whomever we please,'" Eugene Volokh, a law professor emeritus at UCLA who specializes in First Amendment issues, told me in September. "That would spell, at least, if not the end of anti-discrimination law, at least very broad challenges to anti-discrimination law….As a libertarian matter, one could argue that there should be such a right, but the Supreme Court has repeatedly rejected any such claim."
In an appeal to the Supreme Court, Olympus Spa renews its First Amendment claim. Yet it also leans heavily into another argument emphasizing religious exemptions. The spa's owners are devout Christians and, according to their petition, "hold the religious conviction that men and women should not be unclothed together unless married to each other." Consequently, they maintain the spa should be exempt from public accommodations laws insofar as they apply to its single-sex admissions policy.
That is still not a slam dunk. The case law around religious exemptions is somewhat Wild West–esque. That it's so unsettled, though, may encourage the Supreme Court to take a look.
Washington state appears to want to avoid that, if its vote to update the law is any indication. "In the limited circumstance where a business requires nudity as a central purpose of the business," the addition reads, "such business may maintain a rule that entry to spaces where nudity is required be based on genital characteristics." After the vote, the executive director was to work with the Office of the Attorney General to officially file the rule.
That victory may be more superficial than it looks. Nor does it seem likely to deter the business from pushing forward with its appeal. "The Spa is still weighing the legal effect of the Commission's actions," says a source familiar with the litigation. "To begin, the Commission does not have the power to change state law, so it's unclear how much protection—if any—this rule change will give the Spa if a male sues under the Washington Law Against Discrimination for access to areas where the Spa's nude, female patrons congregate. In addition, the Spa's complaint sought nominal damages and is entitled to have its case reinstated to pursue that relief."
The story, while niche, has elicited some strong reactions. "This is a case about swinging dicks," wrote Judge Lawrence VanDyke of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit in March. "You may think that swinging dicks shouldn't appear in a judicial opinion. You're not wrong. But as much as you might understandably be shocked and displeased to merely encounter that phrase in this opinion, I hope we all can agree that it is far more jarring for the unsuspecting and exposed women at Olympus Spa—some as young as thirteen—to be visually assaulted by the real thing."
However crass the phrasing, the fact that Olympus Spa's request—that it not be forced to admit customers with penises to its all-female nude space—has led to such a prolonged battle in the courts understandably strikes many as, well, odd at best. It epitomizes how our legal architecture is sometimes ill-equipped to address commonsense, good-faith objections, even if this example is an edge case.
Yet it also serves as a memorable reminder that resolutions to such disputes often emerge not from the courts but from the people who make the rules. The commission's alteration is a start, though how much protection it really offers remains to be seen. But a more lasting change could come from the Legislature. After Olympus Spa's loss at the 9th Circuit last year, Volokh told me that the most apt remedy would be to go to the source: Amend WLAD. It should be possible, he said, to allow "places of public accommodation to segregate facilities by gender however the places define it," like by anatomy. Sometimes, alas, the threat of a lawsuit is what it takes to get things moving.
The post The Legal Battle Over Who Gets To Show Their Genitals at a Nude Spa Takes an Unexpected Turn appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Milei Campaigned on Dollarizing Argentina. As President, He Stopped Talking About It.
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
Argentina has spent 80 years failing to keep its currency stable. During the 2023 presidential campaign, Javier Milei promised a reform to stop the pattern: abolish the peso and adopt the dollar.
Dollarization was central to his platform. Argentina's monetary institutions had failed too many times to be trusted again. The solution, he said, was to take the currency out of the Argentine government's hands altogether. More than two years later, the peso is still here, and as president, Milei has largely stopped talking about the dollarization he once saw as essential.
Milei's government has made real progress against inflation. Monthly inflation has fallen from 25.5 percent when Milei took office to roughly 2 percent today. That's a genuine achievement. But inflation fell faster under both Ecuador's dollarization in 2000 and Argentina's own currency board in the early 1990s, and neither coincided with a recession as severe as Argentina's recent one.
Dollarization was meant to keep today's progress from becoming just another stabilization that failed to survive the next election. Why did it disappear from Milei's agenda?
The standard advice to a country with Argentina's problems is to do what its more economically stable neighbors do: run a sound fiscal policy, let an independent central bank manage the currency, and allow inflation to fall over time. Peru, Uruguay, and Chile have all followed versions of that path.
Argentina has tried it too. Repeatedly. In the 1990s it adopted a currency board, and beginning in 2016 it tried inflation targeting under a well-regarded central bank. Both were technically reasonable, but each ended in a currency crisis that made future stabilization efforts harder to trust.
The problem was never a shortage of competent technocrats. Argentina keeps alternating between two economic policy regimes: One government stabilizes the currency and balances the budget, then a populist party takes over, prints money to fund spending the country can't afford, wrecks the currency, and loses power. The gap between the two policy approaches is so wide that no exchange-rate regime is sustainable. Argentina can neither fix nor float its currency. The government that inherits the mess then must convince markets and voters that this time is different, even as it relies on the same institutions that just failed.
The problem isn't that any particular president lacks credibility. The country's institutions lack credibility, and for good reason: Argentines have watched this cycle repeat for 80 years.
That currency board is the closest Argentina has come to formal dollarization. Its collapse is also why a currency board isn't a credible option today. The regime ended in the catastrophic 2001 crisis, when the government changed the law and dismantled the peg. Argentines learned that a fixed exchange rate is only as durable as a government's willingness to uphold it. The idea behind formal dollarization is to close this vulnerability.
Dollarization takes the currency out of politicians' hands. Abandoning a fixed exchange rate can take little more than a phone call. Reversing dollarization would mean reintroducing a currency no one wants, an act far more radical and visible than merely abandoning a peg.
That means dollarization can cut inflation without the drawn-out output loss associated with a gradual, reversible disinflation. When people believe a regime truly can't be undone, they stop planning around a future devaluation rather than waiting to see whether the government finishes the job.
Wealthy Argentines and large firms have spent decades building defenses against their own currency: dollar accounts abroad, inflation-indexed contracts, ensuring the ability to reprice quickly when costs rise. Most people who can afford to opt out of the peso already have. Many economists describe Argentina as "informally dollarized": The dollar is the currency that Argentines actually save in, though it lacks legal-tender status.
But not everyone can opt out. A small business owner must hold pesos to make payroll, buy inventory, and pay taxes. A family living paycheck to paycheck may have little opportunity to save in a foreign currency. When monthly inflation reaches double digits, a peso earned on Monday can be worth meaningfully less by Friday. The people least able to reprice, hedge, or convert are the ones who absorb that loss in full.
There's a less visible cost too. Every hour a small business owner spends repricing inventory, chasing a dollar hedge, or tracking shifting exchange rates is an hour not spent serving customers or improving the business. Inflation taxes not just savings but attention.
Currency controls compound the problem. Small importers who need dollars to buy inputs from abroad have often had to navigate a maze of exchange restrictions and multiple exchange rates just to run their businesses, while larger firms with financial sophistication and political access find workarounds.
Inflation falls hardest on people with the fewest tools to escape it. Dollarization would help every Argentine business and household, but most of all those with no way to protect themselves.
If the case for dollarization is this straightforward, why didn't Milei go through with it? The most charitable explanation is that his government never fully understood how to carry out a dollarization plan.
In a 2025 interview, Economy Minister Luis Caputo said dollarization had been ruled out because Argentina lacked enough dollars. That claim doesn't hold up. Countries that have dollarized, such as Ecuador in 2000 and El Salvador in 2001, didn't need to convert every sucre or colón into dollars on day one. Physical currency was exchanged gradually, over periods ranging from nine months to two years, while bank deposits and tax payments were redenominated into dollars almost immediately. In Ecuador, the central bank's own dollar reserves grew during the transition rather than shrank.
The government's on-again, off-again interest in a 100 percent bank reserve requirement—a policy no dollarized economy has ever actually run at scale—points in the same direction. Ecuador also dollarized amid a banking collapse and a default, conditions considerably worse than anything Argentina faced when Milei took office. If Ecuador could do it under those circumstances, then Argentina could have done so at the start of Milei's term and could certainly do so now, from a stronger position than it had at the outset. The constraint was political, not technical.
A May 2026 International Monetary Fund report found that Argentina's gradual disinflation path would require roughly a decade of sustained discipline to succeed. With another presidential election in 2027, there is no guarantee the strategy will remain in place long enough to succeed.
None of this means Milei's stabilization program is doomed, or that dollarization was ever guaranteed to succeed. But two good years, even four, are no substitute for a lasting solution, and a legacy built on a temporary stabilization is not a legacy at all—it is a preface to the next crisis. Workers and small-business owners bear the brunt of every currency crisis, and they have heard versions of "this time is different" before. Whether Milei is remembered as the president who ended that pattern or merely postponed it may depend on a reform he has stopped talking about.

articles.title: Border Search of Immigration Lawyer's Phone Was Likely Unconstitutional Retaliation for Lawyer's Speech
articles.content:
From Judge Allison Burroughs (D. Mass.) Friday in Lattarulo v. Mullin:
Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters," which regularly "amasses hundreds of thousands of views." Georges Cote is currently being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations ("HSI"), the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), for employing individuals without a legal right to work in the United States.
Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025. Unlike Lattarulo, "Cote is not an immigration attorney—he focuses on personal injury." The firm responded on September 12, 2025, and the government sent Cote a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, 2025. The firm was given ten days to attempt to verify the identity and work authorization of the employees named in the Notice of Suspect Documents.
In late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip. On September 27, 2025, Cote arrived back at Logan Airport from Aruba without issue. Lattarulo made the same journey the following day, September 28, 2025. Lattarulo passed through customs preclearance in Aruba before boarding a flight to Boston.
When his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP") agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.
The seized cell phone data is currently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits. The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo's clients. {The Government was clear that any search of the contents of the phone would utilize a taint team to protect privileged information.} …
The court held that Lattarulo was likely correct on his claim that the search was unconstitutional retaliation for his speech, and therefore granted "a preliminary injunction enjoining Defendants from accessing the data obtained from the phone before this action is resolved":
"[T]he law is settled that as a general matter the First Amendment prohibits government officials from subjecting an individual to retaliatory actions, including criminal prosecutions, for speaking out." … The retaliation issue [here] turns on causation—that is, whether the seizure and search of Lattarulo's cell phone would have occurred but for his protected speech.
Respondents have provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise. Indeed, Lattarulo's evidence suggests that any pursuit of criminal charges against employers for employing unauthorized immigrants is exceedingly rare. The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual.
The stage of the investigation at which the search occurred further bolsters the inference of pretext. Under HSI's own policies, the agency "presumes that employers who, within 10 business days of receiving a Notice of Suspect Documents, verify the identity and/or employment authorization of the listed employees, or take appropriate actions to address the apparent employment of unauthorized workers, have demonstrated reasonable care under the INA." The government's search occurred only three days after Georges Cote first received a Notice of Suspect Documents, meaning that the agency was still early in its period of "presum[ing]" compliance when it occurred. Thus, the government's actions here required it to short-circuit its orderly investigative procedures and cast aside its ten-day presumption of compliance in favor of immediately seizing Lattarulo's phone. That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive.
Further, Lattarulo has identified an "otherwise similarly situated individual not engaged in the same sort of protected speech," who was not subjected to the same enforcement action: his law firm partner Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights. Indeed, if the government was truly intent on seizing evidence at the first possible opportunity, Mr. Cote, who returned to America a full day before Lattarulo, would have been a more logical target. Nonetheless, the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search. The balance of the evidence currently before the Court thus suggests that Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech.
{It is true that the presence of probable cause generally precludes a finding of causation in a retaliatory arrest case, but the Supreme Court has recognized a limited exception for situations in which officers who "have probable cause to make arrests [for a particular crime] … typically exercise their discretion not to do so," such as "an individual who has been vocally complaining about police conduct … [before being] arrested for jaywalking," By analogy, the limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here and that Lattarulo's own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property.}
It is true that Defendants can "prevail … by showing that the [search] would have been initiated without respect to retaliation," and here Defendants state that they have additional evidence which would show as much, but they have not provided it because they assert that doing so would prejudice an ongoing investigation…. [T]he Court concludes that the limited record that is before the Court suggests that Lattarulo is likely to succeed on the merits of his First Amendment retaliation claim and that the record before it is therefore adequate to grant the limited preliminary relief contemplated by this order.
The court didn't resolve Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim, because it granted the preliminary injunction based on the First Amendment claim. But it did note the following:
Plaintiffs' Fourth Amendment claim turns largely on the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement. That exception "is grounded in the government's 'inherent authority to protect, and a paramount interest in protecting, its territorial integrity.'" It allows the government to perform "routine" border searches of electronic devices without suspicion of any crime, and to perform "non-routine" border searches of electronic devices without a warrant, so long as the government has reasonable suspicion. Alasaad v. Mayorkas (1st Cir. 2021).
The question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband" or for "evidence of contraband or a border-related crime." Later in its opinion, however, it stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband, evidence of contraband, or for evidence of activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE." In most cases, of course, "border-related crime[s]" and "activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" are synonymous, and the First Circuit in Alasaad appears to have intended to use those terms more or less synonymously.
The difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at issue—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is "enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" but arguably is not a "border-related crime." Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo's border crossing (or, more broadly, the government's interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government's border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.
Even though the suspected violation involves aliens and a law administered by ICE, the Court is not convinced that the First Circuit in Alasaad intended for the border exception to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception. Nonetheless, given the novelty of these questions and the fact that a ruling on them is not necessary, the Court will refrain at this point from reaching a firm conclusion on the issue of the border search's applicability….
Mary Lemay and Patrick M. Hanley (Butters Brazilian LLP) represent Lattarulo.

From Judge Allison Burroughs (D. Mass.) Friday in Lattarulo v. Mullin:

Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters," which regularly "amasses hundreds of thousands of views." Georges Cote is currently being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations ("HSI"), the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), for employing individuals without a legal right to work in the United States.

Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025. Unlike Lattarulo, "Cote is not an immigration attorney—he focuses on personal injury." The firm responded on September 12, 2025, and the government sent Cote a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, 2025. The firm was given ten days to attempt to verify the identity and work authorization of the employees named in the Notice of Suspect Documents.

In late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip. On September 27, 2025, Cote arrived back at Logan Airport from Aruba without issue. Lattarulo made the same journey the following day, September 28, 2025. Lattarulo passed through customs preclearance in Aruba before boarding a flight to Boston.

When his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP") agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

The seized cell phone data is currently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits. The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo's clients. {The Government was clear that any search of the contents of the phone would utilize a taint team to protect privileged information.} …

The court held that Lattarulo was likely correct on his claim that the search was unconstitutional retaliation for his speech, and therefore granted "a preliminary injunction enjoining Defendants from accessing the data obtained from the phone before this action is resolved":

"[T]he law is settled that as a general matter the First Amendment prohibits government officials from subjecting an individual to retaliatory actions, including criminal prosecutions, for speaking out." … The retaliation issue [here] turns on causation—that is, whether the seizure and search of Lattarulo's cell phone would have occurred but for his protected speech.

Respondents have provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise. Indeed, Lattarulo's evidence suggests that any pursuit of criminal charges against employers for employing unauthorized immigrants is exceedingly rare. The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual.

The stage of the investigation at which the search occurred further bolsters the inference of pretext. Under HSI's own policies, the agency "presumes that employers who, within 10 business days of receiving a Notice of Suspect Documents, verify the identity and/or employment authorization of the listed employees, or take appropriate actions to address the apparent employment of unauthorized workers, have demonstrated reasonable care under the INA." The government's search occurred only three days after Georges Cote first received a Notice of Suspect Documents, meaning that the agency was still early in its period of "presum[ing]" compliance when it occurred. Thus, the government's actions here required it to short-circuit its orderly investigative procedures and cast aside its ten-day presumption of compliance in favor of immediately seizing Lattarulo's phone. That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive.

Further, Lattarulo has identified an "otherwise similarly situated individual not engaged in the same sort of protected speech," who was not subjected to the same enforcement action: his law firm partner Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights. Indeed, if the government was truly intent on seizing evidence at the first possible opportunity, Mr. Cote, who returned to America a full day before Lattarulo, would have been a more logical target. Nonetheless, the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search. The balance of the evidence currently before the Court thus suggests that Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech.

{It is true that the presence of probable cause generally precludes a finding of causation in a retaliatory arrest case, but the Supreme Court has recognized a limited exception for situations in which officers who "have probable cause to make arrests [for a particular crime] … typically exercise their discretion not to do so," such as "an individual who has been vocally complaining about police conduct … [before being] arrested for jaywalking," By analogy, the limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here and that Lattarulo's own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property.}

It is true that Defendants can "prevail … by showing that the [search] would have been initiated without respect to retaliation," and here Defendants state that they have additional evidence which would show as much, but they have not provided it because they assert that doing so would prejudice an ongoing investigation…. [T]he Court concludes that the limited record that is before the Court suggests that Lattarulo is likely to succeed on the merits of his First Amendment retaliation claim and that the record before it is therefore adequate to grant the limited preliminary relief contemplated by this order.
